content.text: A small fire against the dark is not much of an argument, but it is the only one available most winter nights. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished.

Walking alone in snow teaches a particular kind of attention, since every sound behind you might be the only one for miles. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down.

I have come to think the coast in winter tells the truth more often than the coast in summer bothers to. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering.

The gulls that stay through December earn a grudging respect from the ones who do not. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time.

A single lit window across the bay becomes, by February, a fixed point I check for before I check anything else. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun.

Meditation, out here, is mostly just cold feet and a willingness to keep walking regardless. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight.

The waves in winter arrive with less patience and more insistence, as though they too were cold. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing.

I burn driftwood because it is what the shore provides, and because it burns with a colour nothing else quite manages. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried.

A path across the dunes disappears under the first real snow and reappears, unhurried, sometime in March. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else.

The winter coast keeps fewer visitors and, I think, more honest ones. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first.

I have walked the shingle at every hour of a December day and found the four in the afternoon light the hardest to describe. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two.

A small fire needs tending more than it needs fuel, which is a lesson that took me longer than it should have. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.

The cold has a way of narrowing a person's thoughts down to the essential handful, and I do not always mind that. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud.

Snow on the dunes holds footprints longer than snow anywhere else I have walked, out of some trick of the wind. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn. The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it.

By the shortest day the light lasts barely long enough to walk the headland and back before dark overtakes it. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

I keep a small fire and a smaller store of patience, and some winters one runs out well before the other. A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed.

The coast in December does not ask to be admired, which is, I have decided, part of what I admire about it. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it.

Walking alone teaches you the sound of your own breathing in a way company never quite allows. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.

A winter meditation, if it is honest, ends without a conclusion, only a walk back toward the fire. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting.

The tide in December comes in grey and leaves grey, and I have learned not to expect it to announce a mood. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished.

An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind.

The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last.

A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true.

The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud.

An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood.

The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening.
